one_liner: Java-written optimizing JIT that replaces HotSpot's C2; 16% lower time-per-op geomean than C2 on a third-party JMH compiler suite.
what_it_does: The Graal compiler is the top-tier JIT of GraalVM distributions and can stand in for C2 in any JVMCI-enabled HotSpot (in Oracle JDK via -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseGraalJIT). It is not a library you link: you switch JDK distribution or JVM flags and your Java code runs unchanged. It normally ships as libgraal, a Native Image shared library, so the compiler itself does not live on the Java heap or need to warm up; the same compiler also backs Native Image and the Truffle language runtimes.
how_it_is_fast: It compiles from a graph IR with speculative optimizations backed by deoptimization, partial escape analysis (an object is allocated only on the paths where it escapes), aggressive and polymorphic inlining (a call-graph-wide PriorityInliningPhase became the default in 25.3), and path duplication (DBDS, CGO 2018). The 25.x community configuration has also gained loop vectorization, lock coarsening and elimination of nested locks, partial redundancy elimination scheduling, write sinking and aggressive partial unrolling. The suite's largest wins come from these: nested synchronized blocks at 0.48 ns vs C2 196 ns, a megamorphic virtual call chain at 0.8-3.5 ns vs 37.6 ns, and non-escaping objects scalar-replaced (0.61 ns vs 11.5 ns).
when_to_use: Long-running, throughput-bound JVM services where steady-state peak matters more than startup, and where you can A/B the same build with -XX:-UseJVMCICompiler.

Abstraction-heavy Java with many short-lived objects (streams, lambdas, iterators, boxed values), where partial escape analysis removes allocations; in the suite's program category GameOfLife iterative ran at 0.49x C2's time, LZW decompress 0.52x and dynamic-programming knapsack 0.59x.
Code with megamorphic interface or virtual call chains, or redundant/nested locking, where the inliner and lock optimizations remove most of the cost.
Hosting Truffle languages (GraalJS, GraalPy, Espresso), which depend on this compiler for their JIT.

Teams already on GraalVM CE for JDK 25: per the compiler CHANGELOG, optimizations that used to be Oracle-only (loop vectorization, duplication) are now in the open-source community configuration, and in this suite CE and Oracle GraalVM land on the same 0.84.
when_not_to_use: Code whose hot paths rely on C2-specific simplifications: in the same suite Graal is 30,000x slower on DeadLoopEliminationBenchmark.dead_loop (C2 deletes the loop, 0.61 ns vs 18,233 ns), 8,800x on any_true_array_element, 153x on NpeControlFlowBenchmark.try_npe_catch, 35-41x on implicit NullPointerException throws, and 3-7x on sequential byte/short/int stores that C2 merges.

Short-lived or cold-start-sensitive processes: the suite measures steady state only, and issue #13387 reports a 27% cold-wall regression vs C2 (4.78 s vs 3.47 s median) from repeated 'COMPILE SKIPPED: Speculation failed' recompiles on Oracle GraalVM 25.0.2.

Workloads where the median benchmark is what matters: the median per-benchmark ratio to C2 is 0.99 in the compiler category, 0.95 in API and 0.96 in programs, so most code sees little change and the geomean comes from a minority of large wins.

Deployments that cannot absorb a less battle-tested top-tier compiler: open issue #14495 (Sept 2026) is a miscompile where a loop that must never terminate returns a finite sum on Oracle GraalVM 25.0.3 and 25.4 (C2 correct).

When pinned to one GraalVM version without testing: on the JDK 21 release of the same suite GraalVM CE was slower than C2 (compiler category 1.06, whole suite 1.03) while Oracle GraalVM was 0.64 and 0.77, so the gain depends heavily on edition and release.

integration.form: shared lib (libgraal inside a GraalVM JDK distribution; or experimental -XX:+UseGraalJIT in Oracle JDK); jargraal runs as ordinary Java on the heap
integration.dependencies: A JVMCI-enabled JDK (GraalVM CE/Oracle GraalVM, or LabsJDK when building from source); the mx build tool to build it yourself
integration.min_toolchain: JDK 17+ (GR-42212 removed support for older JDKs); current master is built against LabsJDK 25 (jvmci-25.1-b14 in vm/README.md)
integration.platforms: AMD64 and AArch64 back ends (both named in compiler/CHANGELOG.md); the cited suite measured x86_64 only
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable as a library; compiles on background JVMCI threads whose default count matches C2's since GraalVM for JDK 24 (-XX:JVMCINativeLibraryThreadFraction=0.66), which can raise peak RSS
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — no source changes, but you switch JDK distribution or add experimental flags; C2-specific -XX tuning flags do not apply and Graal is tuned with -Djdk.graal.* properties

gotchas: Harness flaw in the cited suite: scripts/ggplot2/geomean-utils.r converts s/ms/us scores to ns but leaves 12 throughput-mode rows (ops/s, from ColumnarDBFilterBenchmark and VectorizedScanOperationBenchmark) in the lower-is-better geomean, so Graal's throughput losses count as wins (vectorized_query_IS_EVEN_pivot at size 1048576: HotSpot 3356 ops/s vs Graal 466 ops/s is scored as a 7x Graal gain). Recomputed from the committed CSVs, the API category is 0.93 rather than the published 0.92 and the whole suite 0.904; the compiler-category 0.84 (reproduced as 0.835 over 298 rows) has no throughput rows and is unaffected.

The geomean depends on a few extreme results. In the compiler category 116 of 298 rows are more than 5% faster than C2 and 74 more than 5% slower; dropping rows outside a 0.2x-5x ratio gives 0.94 instead of 0.84, and per-class equal weighting gives 0.75. The script also divides one geomean of raw scores by another rather than matching rows by name; the row sets happen to be identical here.

Edition and version matter more than the docs suggest: the reference Options.md still says vectorization and the 'enterprise' configuration are Oracle GraalVM only, but compiler/CHANGELOG.md moves those optimizations into the community compiler during the 25.x series, and in this JDK 25 run 991 of 1136 rows are within 2% between CE and Oracle GraalVM. The suite records neither the exact GraalVM releases nor -Djdk.graal.ShowConfiguration output, so which optimizations ran cannot be confirmed.

jargraal (the compiler running as plain Java) allocates on the application heap, can increase GC pauses and starts interpreted; use libgraal, as the GraalVM builds do, unless you are debugging the compiler.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose Graal over Eclipse OpenJ9 when steady-state peak throughput of abstraction-heavy Java matters more than startup and footprint, which is where OpenJ9's catalogued advantage (about 40% faster startup with a shared-class-cache AOT) lies. It is also the compiler underneath the catalogued Graal.js, so pick it whenever you run Truffle languages.
verified_claims_summary: ionutbalosin/jvm-performance-benchmarks (JMH average time, 5 forks of 5 x 10 s measurement iterations after 5 x 10 s warmup, -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, JDK 25 on an unnamed x86_64 machine, exact builds not stated) puts GraalVM CE's JIT at a time-per-op geomean of 0.84 of OpenJDK HotSpot C2 over 298 compiler-pattern microbenchmarks, and the GraalVM CE VM at 0.90 over all 1136. Recomputing from the committed per-benchmark CSVs gives 0.835 for the compiler category; correcting the throughput-row direction gives 0.904 for the whole suite.
status_note: Very active (commits on 2026-10-06, frequent compiler changes between 25.x releases); the compiler is GPL-2.0 with Classpath Exception in GraalVM CE, and Oracle GraalVM builds carry separate licence terms. You adopt it by switching JDK, not by vendoring code.
